description: GAIA is a team passionate about Earth observation, space technology, and turning SAR data into real-world insights. We’re a collaborative group of curious builders, researchers, and problem-solvers looking to combine science, technology, and creativity.
summary:
What we developed

GAIA CascadeLens is a free, offline, browser-based evidence explorer for the 26 August 2026 Rasuwa–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli disaster in Nepal, with a second case on the Tsho Rolpa glacial lake. It puts real NISAR radar products (GUNW, GOFF and GCOV) on a map, alongside terrain, UNOSAT and Sentinel-1 layers. A Python pipeline runs quality checks and records provenance before the data reaches a static web app. Every layer and figure carries an evidence class, a quality rating and its limits. The app also includes a “Can the radar see it?” tool, a rule-based explanation panel, field-check records and printable evidence reports.

How it addresses the challenge

For “Dancing with the SARs”, it turns NISAR data into something people can inspect. Coherence along the mapped channel is 0.19, against 0.46 on nearby terrain. At the detachment zone, neither viewing direction can measure movement, and the app says so. It calculates no displacement.

Why it matters

Radar products are easy to over-read. CascadeLens shows where NISAR can and cannot help after a cascading hazard. It separates observation from inference, so responders and researchers can see what to trust and what to check next.
details:
What it does

This interactive web map turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into clear, accessible evidence for monitoring glacial lakes and mountain hazards in the Nepal Himalayas. Featuring a deep dive into the 2026 Rasuwa event along the Trishuli corridor—as well as Tsho Rolpa lake—the platform compares ascending and descending radar passes to pinpoint where the ground surface has shifted. Just as importantly, it clearly highlights areas where the data is too uncertain to make a call. Users can also explore the terrain in 3D or run simulations to test different lake and downstream flow scenarios.

Benefits & impact

Because radar penetrates heavy cloud cover, this tool works reliably year-round, regardless of the weather. To prevent alarmism and keep the science honest, every data layer is labeled by its maturity level, and events are carefully phrased—such as using "Reported ice and rock avalanche" rather than jumping to conclusions about a lake breach. Ultimately, this is a research and awareness tool designed to help local communities, planners, and emergency responders ask the right questions about downstream risks.

Tools & tech stack

  • Data: NISAR GCOV, GUNW, and GOFF products
  • Processing: Python (h5py, numpy)
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, and MapLibre
  • Deployment: Hosted on GitHub Pages, with a downloadable offline package for fieldwork

Creativity & design choices

Instead of hiding data gaps, we treated uncertainty as a feature—building a dedicated "unable to judge" layer backed by radar coherence checks. We also designed the app for real-world field conditions, adding automatic warnings for poor internet connections and a lightweight mode so it runs smoothly on older laptops and budget smartphones.

Key considerations

Throughout development, we focused on handling strict data limitations (such as the lack of Tsho Rolpa imagery after September 21), verifying radar coherence, keeping language simple and jargon-free, and ensuring the platform remains usable even on weak, rural networks.
